questions.question: Two processes share a pipe, which is just a stream of bytes. What does MCP's stdio transport use to mark where one message ends?
options: A newline: each message is one line of JSON
questions.explanation: JSON escapes newlines inside strings, so a message never contains a raw one.

questions.question: Which message never gets a reply?
options: A request with a string id
A notification (a method with no id)
A request for an unknown method
questions.explanation: Requests always get a result or an error; notifications never do.

questions.question: A client sends a request with no _meta in params to a 2026-07-28 server. What comes back?
questions.explanation: protocolVersion and clientCapabilities in _meta are required on every request.

questions.question: The client sent id 6 then id 7, and the response for 7 arrived first. What should the client do?
options: Treat it as a protocol error
Match each response to its request by id
questions.explanation: Out-of-order responses are normal; the id is the correlation.

questions.question: Why could the server act on the cancel while slow_count was still running?
options: Cancels jump the queue in the pipe
The work ran on its own thread, so the reader loop kept reading lines
questions.explanation: A server that blocks its reader on long work can't see the cancel until the work is done.

questions.question: A Python stdio server works in your tests but hosts keep dropping it. A library it uses prints a warning on startup. Most likely cause?
options: The warning goes to stdout and corrupts the message stream
questions.explanation: Stdout is the protocol channel; every log line must go to stderr.
